notes.key_messages: • In the qualitative analysis question ( Question 2 ), candidates we re expected to use the term ‘precipitate’ when describing the formation of a solid from the reaction between two solutions. If , when two solutions are mixed , the product becomes cloudy and opaque, then a precipitate has been formed. • When a question asks for observations, stating that a gas is given off is not an observation. The relevant observation would be effervescence or fizzing or bubbles (of a gas). Similarly, when asked for observations when a gas has been evolved, identifying the gas is not an observation. The test and the result of the test are needed. • Not all the tests described will necessarily give a positive result; a negative test result is useful since it tells us that a certain ion is not in the compound being tested. • When a question asks for the name of a chemical, a correct formula is always acceptable. However, if a candidate answers with an incorrect formula, then credit will not be awarded. • When plotting graphs, points should be plotted as a cross ( x ) or an encircled dot (  ) and not obscured by the graph line, which should be drawn using a sharp pencil. A line of best fit can be curved or straight – whichever i s the best fit for the data points. Straight lines should be drawn with the aid of a rule and not drawn freehand; curves should be smooth and not just a line which moves from point to point. Graph scales should be chosen such that the plotted data takes up over half of the available spac e and it is recommended that each major grid line should be equivalent to 1, 2, or 5 (or those numbers multiplied by 10 n )° – this is indicated in the Presentation of Data section of the syllabus in the section entitled ‘ Graphs ’ (and also recommended by the Association for Science Education (A.S.E.)). • Readings recorded from a given item of apparatus should all be recorded to the same resolution (the same number of decimal places).
notes.general_comments: The vast majority of candidates successfully attempted all the questions and the full range of marks was seen. Most candidates were able to complete the questions in the time available. The paper discriminated successfully between candidates of different a bilities but was accessible to all and was generally well - answered, with very few blank spaces. In answering the planning question ( Question 3 ) , there is no need for candidates to write a list of apparatus at the start, nor the aims of the experiment, nor a list of safety precautions. Where there is credit available for the use of suitable apparatus, this will only be awarded if it is stated what the apparatus is used for. Credit will not be awarded just for a name in a list of other apparatus. There was evidence to suggest that more practical work was being used in the teaching of this syllabus than has been seen in the last few years.
notes.1a: Most candidates obtained results in line with those expected in that as the volume of aqueous sodium thiosulfate decreased the time taken for the text to not be visible increased. The recording of time to the nearest whole number was done my a large number of candidates . I t is generally not appropriate to quote reaction times in tenths or hundredths of a second for chemistry experiments due to factors like limitations in measurement precision.
notes.1b: Most of the graphs had a suitable scale on the y - axis, usually 2 cm grid square = 10 seconds. Some candidates selected difficult scales where each 2 cm grid square was 1.5 or 3; these candidates often made errors in plotting. Each large grid square should be 1, 2 or 5  10 . The points were generally correctly plotted. There were many who thought that lines of best fit must be straight lines. The curves of best fit were often poorly drawn. S traight sections on a curve of best fit, very thick lines, wobbly lines or any double line where a gap is visible between the lines is not acceptable.
notes.1ci: Candidates performed well on this question and were able to calculate the relative rate using the formula given. Candidates who did not evaluate the fraction gained no credit as there had been no attempt at a calculation.
notes.1cii: This was one of the most accessible questions on the paper and almost all candidates could identify that experiment 1 had the greatest relative rate.
notes.1di: Most candidates were able to calculate the volume of water and give the appropriate unit. Less well performing candidates found this question difficult as they had not understood that the total volume of solution had to remain constant. They often gained credit for units even with an incorrect calculation.
notes.1dii: Nearly all candidates could work out the relevant time for the text to not be visible at 37 cm . To gain full credit , working had to be shown as stated in the question. The clearest working is the use of construction lines. Candidates who performed less well chose the incorrect volume; the most 3 3 common was using 36 or 38.5 cm rather than 37 cm .
notes.1diii: Candidates performed poorly on this question and found it very challenging. Most candidates just restated ‘so that the total volume is kept constant’ or said so that ‘ it is a fair test ’ . Few appreciated that if the total volume changes between experiments, you are introducing a second variable, which would make it unclear whether any changes in reaction rate are due to concentration or to volume.
notes.1ei: This was the most accessible question on the paper with almost all candidates understanding that burettes measure volumes more accurately than measuring cylinders.
notes.1eii: This question was answered well. Candidates were able to state that either pipettes had fixed volumes or that the pipette sizes available were too small and could not hold the larger variable volumes of sodium thiosulfate required. ( f ) This was found to be the most challenging question on the paper and few correct answers were seen. Many candidates incorrectly related their answer to surface area and rate of reaction without realising that a beaker will have a larger cross section and so result in a shallower depth of liquid; t his makes it easier to see through and so it takes more time for the text to be obscured.
notes.2a: The expected observations on solution L with aqueous sodium carbonate were a white precipitate forming and effervescence. Many candidates noted one out of these two. Better performing candidates were guided by the mark allocation of [2] and realised that two observations were expected.
notes.2b: As the question stated that NaOH should be added dropwise and then in excess, candidates should give an observation for each step. As solution L contained an aluminium salt, a white precipitate is form ed on dropwise addition which should dissolve in excess. Some candidates gave answers which suggested they did not mix the contents of the boiling tube when adding in excess and so reported a white precipitate at the bottom and a colourless solution above. A few candidates reported precipitates that were not white, but this is impossible due to solution L containing the aluminium salt.
notes.2c: Similarly, as the question stated that aqueous ammonia should be added dropwise and then in excess, candidates should give an observation for each step. As solution L contained an aluminium salt, a white precipitate is form ed on dropwise addition which should remain excess. Some candidates gave answers which suggested they did not mix the contents of the boiling tube when adding in excess and so reported a white precipitate at the bottom and a colourless solution above – that colourless solution would be aqueous ammonia that has not mixed with the precipitate. Several candidates mixed up the observations for (b) and (c) and care should be taken to note the observations in the correct answer spaces.
notes.2d: Most candidates reported the expected white precipitate. It was not uncommon for candidates to report a cream precipitate. C andidates should be familiar with the colours of silver halide precipitates, comparing the precipitate colour to a sheet of white paper can help determine if the precipitate is white or cream. Some candidates reported that there was no change – the most pr obable reason for this is adding incorrect reagents when they performed the test.
notes.2e: Those candidates who obtained correct observations were generally successful in identifying the salt as aluminium and chloride. Candidates often stated the ions in solid L and this gained full credit, but it should be noted that the term ‘ chlorine ion ’ is not accepted for ‘ chloride ion ’.
notes.2f: The expected flame test colour was green for solid M . Candidates received credit if they gave the expected colour or a colour that matched the supervisor’s results. If the supervisor results for Question 2 are not submitted, then the only accepted answer is the expected colour of green; it is essential that supervisor results are submitted for Q uestions 1 and 2 .
notes.2gi: The test carried out was the test for nitrate ions and the expected result was effervescence and red litmus turning blue. Many candidates gained credit for stating that the gas produced turned red litmus blue but did not state that effervescence was seen. ‘Gas produced’ is not an observation but a conclusion from the effervescence seen. ( ii) Most candidates noted the formation of a white precipitate as solid M was a barium salt.
notes.2h: Candidates who performed well often gained full credit for the identification of solid M as barium nitrate. It was not uncommon for candidates to identify only that solid M contained barium ions and not include an anion in their answer.
